# Guarantee Design — the eight types

> Vendored/condensed from coreyhaines31/marketingskills,
> `skills/offers/references/guarantee-design.md` (MIT license). Kept in
> English per repo convention (dense reference catalog). Used by r-offers
> step 5 (Risiko-Umkehr) to pick the right guarantee shape before drafting —
> German UWG-Einlösbarkeits-Regel in SKILL.md still applies on top of this.

A guarantee raises perceived likelihood of achievement ("they'd only offer
this if confident") and lowers effort/risk. The **wrong** guarantee hurts more
than no guarantee — pick the type that matches the business model, don't
default to generic "money-back."

## The eight types

| # | Type | Promise | Works when | Backfires when |
|---|------|---------|-----------|-----------------|
| 1 | Unconditional money-back | Refund anytime within X days, no questions | Low-priced info, high-trust audience | High-priced/high-touch — refund risk eats margin |
| 2 | Conditional money-back | Refund if buyer completes X and still doesn't see Y | Courses/programs requiring effort | Sophisticated buyers read too many conditions as a trap |
| 3 | Better-than-money-back | Refund + bonus $X if it doesn't work | Confident delivery, ample margin | The rare failure explodes publicly |
| 4 | Service-level / SLA | Money back if we miss a measurable deadline | Productized services, agency work | Vague, unmeasurable SLAs |
| 5 | Performance-based | Pay only when X happens (rev-share, results) | Sophisticated B2B, high delivery confidence | Long cycles, hard-to-attribute outcomes |
| 6 | Anti-guarantee | No refunds, be sure before you buy | Premium, mature, self-qualified buyers | First-time/confused buyers read it as cold |
| 7 | Outcome-or-extension | If no X by Y, we continue free | Coaching/services with extendable time | Open-ended cost if mis-scoped |
| 8 | Comparison guarantee | Beat competitor's result or refund | When you can credibly, cleanly compare | When the comparison can't be measured fairly |

## Picking one — decision tree

1. **Buyer's biggest perceived risk?** "Won't work" → 1/2/3. "Won't deliver on time" → 4. "I pay, no result" → 5 or 7. "Is this real?" → 8.
2. **Refund tolerance?** Can absorb at scale → 1. Need to qualify refunders → 2. Confident enough to add a bonus → 3. Can't afford refunds → 6.
3. **Buyer sophistication?** Premium/mature → anti-guarantee reads as confidence. First-time-in-category → they need permission to try, give a real refund guarantee. Sophisticated B2B → expects SLA/performance terms.
4. **Outcome measurability?** Clean/measurable → performance-based, comparison, outcome-or-extension. Fuzzy → money-back family gated on completed effort.

## Writing it (patterns that work vs. don't)

**Works:** specific conditions ("complete weeks 1–4, still no [named outcome] → full refund"), confident tone ("we know this works; if it doesn't for you, we don't want your money"), acknowledging the awkwardness directly.

**Doesn't:** "100% satisfaction guaranteed" (generic, low-trust), "lifetime guarantee" (meaningless without conditions), stacked guarantees (reads as sophistication-collapsing), legalese (buyers skim and assume the worst).

## Common mistakes

- **Promising more than deliverable** — stress-test: what happens if 10% of buyers invoke the guarantee? A guarantee that bankrupts you at a 10% invoke-rate is the wrong guarantee.
- **Too many conditions** — max two; three only if tightly related. More reads as "designed to be impossible to claim."
- **Hiding it in fine print** — if it's the strongest perceived-likelihood lever, put it above the buy button, not in a footnote.
- **Guarantee as a substitute for proof** — strong proof + weak guarantee beats strong guarantee + weak proof. Build proof first, then layer the guarantee.

## When NO guarantee is honest (anti-guarantee case)

Works when: buyer sophistication is high, an application/qualification step precedes the sale, price is premium, brand is established, proof is overwhelming. The message is "we don't need a guarantee — the work is real, you self-qualified, we won't play refund games." Wrong audience reads this as cold; right audience reads it as confidence.
